capabilities.target: private repositories owned by the user

inputs.source: Issue text in the public repository, authored by any GitHub user

elements.name: GitHub MCP server (dockerized, ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server, unpinned tag)

controls.name: Per-tool-call human approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: The approver sees a model-generated summary with arguments collapsed by default, and approves many calls per session. A more persuasive model can write summaries that obscure a sensitive read, and approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403) sets in under volume, so the gate weakens under model_upgrade and autonomy_increase even though it is enforced outside the model.

controls.name: Least-privilege, per-repository credential scoping
controls.decay_rationale: A credential scoped only to the public repository would make cap.read_private_repo unreachable regardless of model behavior, severing the path. Today the PAT has repo scope across every owned repository, public and private.

controls.name: Pinned/hashed MCP server image
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning the docker image to a digest would prevent silent tool redefinition (rug pull). Today the docker run command references the image by name only, with no tag or digest, so its behavior can change between runs without review.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted public issue drives a private-repo read into a public pull request

attack_path.note: Attacker-authored issue in the public repo contains content/instructions the agent treats as task context
Agent follows the injected content and reads confidential data from a private repository, enabled by the broad-scope PAT shared across all repos
Agent embeds the private content in a pull request opened on the public repository, disclosing it to anyone who can view the repo

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

findings.residual_rationale: Rubric step 2 credit (-2 tiers from critical) floors at moderate, but the only control is a per-call approval prompt that reviews the read and the write as two separately innocuous calls, with arguments collapsed by default, and users approve many such prompts per session (SAFE-T1403 consent fatigue). The approver never sees the read-then-write combination or the private content embedded in the PR. That decoupling is not fully captured by the partially_dependent classification alone, so residual is rated high rather than the moderate floor.

forecast.watch_signal: Model/version string change in the client config; approval policy changed to auto-approve or allow-list mode for this MCP server; rising approvals-per-reviewer-per-hour for this tool.

evidence.observation: mcp.json launches ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server with GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN passed through as the only credential boundary for every call, and no image tag or digest is pinned
The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private, so credential_scope is broad rather than least_privilege
Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository, so issue content is an untrusted (U) input that enters the agent's context
The client approval prompt collapses arguments by default and users approve many calls per session, which is a model_summary review mode subject to approval fatigue

recommendations.action: Issue a fine-grained PAT scoped only to the public repository for this agent; never grant cross-repo or private-repo scope to an agent that also processes public, attacker-reachable content.
Require raw-action approval review (full file path and content read, full PR diff) for any call that crosses a public/private repository boundary, instead of a collapsed model summary.
Pin the MCP server image to a specific digest to prevent unreviewed behavior changes.
Log and alert when a single session reads from a private repository and writes to a public one.

rating.rationale: A single present finding dominates the rating: an untrusted public GitHub issue can drive the agent, via a broadly-scoped PAT, to read a private repository and disclose its contents through a public pull request (U source to S3 sink = inherent critical). The only control is a per-call approval prompt reviewed as a model summary with collapsed arguments and high approval volume, which the rubric credits down to a moderate floor but which is judged to leave residual at high because the two calls are approved independently and the combination is invisible to the reviewer. Under model_upgrade, autonomy_increase, or control_removal, this partially_dependent gate is expected to fail outright, returning the finding to its critical inherent level, which sets the forecast rating.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior; no live session logs, actual approval-prompt UI, or git history were reviewed.
No system prompt was provided beyond the single user request shown; instruction-level issues (ambiguous_goal, unbounded_scope, etc.) could not be fully evaluated.

Whether the docker image is pulled from a cache versus the registry at run time, and whether any organization-level image allowlist exists outside these artifacts, is unknown; confidence on the supply-chain/pinning observation is medium.

Approval volume per reviewer per day is not quantified in the artifacts; the approval-fatigue judgment is based on the stated pattern (collapsed arguments, many approvals per session) rather than a measured rate.
